mainEntity.name: How much does a Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A full rebuilt or reconditioned engine for the Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi typically costs between £1,200 and £4,000 for the unit alone, depending on whether it is the U2 1.1L or R2 1.4L code. Used engines start around £400. Reconditioned units range from £1,200 to £2,800. Supply and fit labour adds approximately £500 to £900 depending on the specialist.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of timing chain failure in a Hyundai i20 1.4 CRDi?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common early warning sign is a distinct rattling or ticking noise from the engine bay during a cold startup, which may fade as the engine warms up. Other signs include loss of engine power, rough running, and illumination of the check engine light. In severe cases, it can cause catastrophic internal damage if the chain snaps.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a 2009-2014 Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends entirely on the current market value of your specific vehicle, which typically ranges from £1,500 to £5,000. If the car is worth under £5,000, a used engine or targeted repair is usually the most financially sensible route. A full rebuilt engine is only recommended if you plan to keep the car for several more years and want the peace of mind of a 12-month warranty.

mainEntity.name: How long does a Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi engine replacement take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A professional supply and fit service for the Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi typically takes between 1 to 2 working days. This includes engine removal and preparation (4-6 hours), installation, fluid refills, and ECU reset (4-6 hours), and road testing with final quality checks (1-2 hours).

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi and 1.4 CRDi engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 1.1 CRDi (U2 engine) produces 75hp and is focused purely on maximum fuel economy and low tax bands, but is more prone to EGR clogging. The 1.4 CRDi (R2 engine) produces 90hp, offering better overtaking power, but carries a known risk of timing chain stretch between 60,000 and 100,000 miles.

historyTimeline.h2: Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: When the 1.1 CRDi and 1.4 CRDi variants launched in the first-generation (PB) Hyundai i20, they provided highly economical diesel options for UK buyers, though the 1.4L variant later became known for specific timing chain vulnerabilities requiring careful maintenance.

milestones.description: U2 1.1L CRDi (75hp) and R2 1.4L CRDi (90hp) introduced for the PB generation, offering strong fuel economy and low tax bands.
Minor emissions and EGR system updates applied to the U2 1.1L CRDi to improve reliability and meet evolving Euro 5 standards.
End of production for the PB generation diesel variants; replaced by the GB generation with updated engine families, phasing out the R2 1.4 CRDi architecture.

historyTimeline.closingNote: Every engine fitted to the Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi is covered below, with UK rebuilt pricing and known failure points to help you make an informed replacement decision.

commonProblems.h2: Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The reliability picture for the Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi is generally defined by two distinct issues: EGR complexity in the 1.1L U2 engine, and timing chain vulnerability in the 1.4L R2 engine. Rebuilt engines sourced through EnginesMarket include upgraded components addressing these original failure points, backed by a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: R2 1.4 CRDi Timing Chain Stretch - Why the Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi R2 Engine Wears Prematurely
problems.rootCause: Premature wear of the timing chain and tensioner assembly, causing a distinct rattling noise on cold startup and risking catastrophic valve-to-piston collision if the chain skips or snaps.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replaces timing chain, guides, and tensioner.
repairOptions.longevity: Suitable only if caught early via startup rattle, before internal damage occurs.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit, upgraded components addressing the original failure point, 12-month warranty.
repairOptions.longevity: The right call when catastrophic internal damage has already occurred.

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2009-2014 Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi is currently valued between £1,500 and £5,000 `[THIRD-PARTY]`. - Vehicle worth under ~£5,000: repair or a used engine typically makes more financial sense than a full rebuilt unit. - *Honest note*: If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing.
problems.recommendation: For the R2 1.4 CRDi, if you hear a startup rattle, address the timing chain immediately with a specialist kit to avoid catastrophic failure. Only opt for a full rebuilt engine if the block is already damaged or you firmly plan to keep the vehicle long-term.

problems.h4: U2 1.1 CRDi EGR & Injector Issues - Why the Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi U2 Engine Loses Power
problems.rootCause: Carbon buildup in the EGR valve and degradation of injector seals, leading to poor idle, loss of power, and rough running, especially in urban driving conditions.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Cleans or replaces EGR valve and checks injector seals.
repairOptions.longevity: Highly suitable for early-stage clogging and restores drivability.
Recommended only if injector failure has caused secondary internal damage.

problems.vehicleValueCheck: As noted above, the £1,500-£5,000 value band of the Hyundai i20 1.1 CRDi / 1.4 CRDi means a full rebuild is rarely cost-effective unless the vehicle has exceptional condition or sentimental value.
problems.recommendation: For the U2 1.1 CRDi, regular EGR cleaning and using high-quality diesel additives are highly cost-effective preventative measures. A full engine replacement is rarely justified for EGR issues alone unless secondary damage is confirmed.
